claims.text: The ethanol-oxidation performance of the PGM nanoscale catalyst is governed by in situ formation of a controlled sub-monolayer of surface oxide/hydroxide species.
A surface oxide/hydroxide sub-monolayer fine-tunes the adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The oxide/hydroxide sub-monolayer facilitates the 12-electron/12-proton ethanol-oxidation process.
The target catalyst has well-dispersed PGM active sites on a support.
Strongly reducing electrochemical conditions minimize surface oxide/hydroxide formation on the target catalyst.
Changing from strongly reducing to moderately oxidizing potential induces a controlled oxide/hydroxide sub-monolayer.
The oxide/hydroxide layer modulates the catalyst's surface electronic structure.
Under moderately oxidizing conditions, a stable oxide/hydroxide sub-monolayer forms on the catalyst.
The sub-monolayer adjusts adsorption and desorption energies of adsorbed CO and oxygenated intermediates.
Optimization of intermediate binding by the sub-monolayer lowers the activation energy of ethanol oxidation.
The proposed adsorption optimization enhances catalytic activity.
The proposed surface sub-monolayer increases selectivity toward complete ethanol-oxidation products.
The proposed surface sub-monolayer improves catalyst durability.
Absence of the oxide/hydroxide layer under strongly reducing conditions causes suboptimal intermediate adsorption and lower performance.
Moderately oxidizing operation will produce higher ethanol-oxidation current density than strongly reducing operation.
Moderately oxidizing operation will improve selectivity for complete ethanol oxidation relative to the reducing baseline.
Moderately oxidizing operation will improve long-term durability relative to the reducing baseline.
More strongly oxidizing potentials form thick or passivating oxide layers that suppress the proposed mechanism.
Prior evidence from analogous ORR systems supports controlled surface oxidation as a means of optimizing intermediate adsorption.
